newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Americans to join evacuation from Sierra Leone.
newsitem.headline: Americans to join evacuation from Sierra Leone.

text.p: The United States will fly about 250 of its nationals out of Sierra Leone on Friday ahead of an expected intervention by Nigerian troops to restore the civilian president ousted in a coup last weekend.
Nigeria flew in more troops and supplies on Thursday to join hundreds already in place under a plan by West African leaders to reinstate ousted president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.

The U.S. Navy helicopter ship Kearsarge, which steamed north to Freetown from waters off former Zaire, prepared to fly out about 250 Americans on Friday but Washington turned down a plea for the 1,200 Marines on board to help overturn the coup.
As a foreign exodus gathered pace, a Boeing 747 carrying 392 mostly European evacuees left for London on Thursday.
They dived for cover after a shot rang out as they boarded the plane, but no one was hurt in the confrontation between Nigerian and Sierra Leonean troops.

Sierra Leonean troops have allowed the Nigerians to continue controlling Lungi international airport, which has been under their care as part of regional accords on peacekeeping in neighbouring Liberia.
However, their relationship since the coup has been described as "correct but not cordial".

"There was a confrontation between the two sides who control opposite ends of the runway. A shot was fired as the evacuees were queueing to board the plane and everyone took defensive positions on the tarmac," a British diplomat told Reuters.
He said the shot had been fired by a Sierra Leonean soldier.
Witnesses said the incident was exacerbated by the Sierra Leoneans' refusal to allow a Nigerian C-130 Hercules to land with troops and supplies. The Nigerians insisted on landing the plane.

Sierra Leone's ambassador to the United States, John Leigh, told a rally of Sierra Leoneans in Washington he was urging the U.S. administration "to work with other nations and international organisations to act decisively to end the crisis, by force of arms if necessary."

But State Department spokesman John Dinger said the role of the Kearsarge, which is lying about 20 miles (32 km) offshore, was only to evacuate American citizens, who will be flown on to Conakry, capital of neighbouring Guinea.
About 700 foreign nationals flew out of Freetown on Wednesday and Thursday.

"It wasn't the welcome I had hoped for," said Canadian George Cone, 42, from Calgary, who arrived only a week ago on his first trip to Africa to organise training for a cellular phone company setting up a network in Sierra Leone. He flew out on the British-chartered jumbo jet.
The coup appears to have little public support, though rebel leader Foday Sankoh on Wednesday called on his forces to support the army against the Nigerians if necessary.
Trade unions and other civil groups have asked people to stay at home in protest against the coup. Shops and offices have stayed closed all week.
The new military authorities who seized power on Sunday blamed harassment of civilians on former servicemen and escaped prisoners in army uniform and warned they would be arrested.
The most prominent escaped prisoner is the new head of state, Major Johnny Paul Koromah.

Koromah, 33, was among those freed from Freetown's Pademba Road prison early on Sunday at the start of the coup. He was detained on treason charges over an earlier alleged coup attempt against Kabbah, who flew to Guinea on Sunday.
